Generic magnetic reorientation activates the second component and tunes both components through positive and negative values. Global reversal preserves the dipole while reversing the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity, allowing a finite bulk dipole contribution from equally populated reversed domains under uniform-field averaging.A symmetry-constrained polynomial model predicts both dipole components for 256 held-out spin configurations, achieving coefficients of determination $R^2 > 0.9995$ at the reference chemical potential. At fixed carrier density, orientation-dependent shifts of the chemical potential modify the response and yield slightly larger prediction errors for the chosen model. Across the chemical-potential sweep,the prediction accuracy decreases more strongly for $D_y$,revealing an energy dependence of the surrogate's performance. Within semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the calculated dipole determines the angular dependence of the quadratic current and its rectified and second-harmonic components. These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $α$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.

title: Grain-Boundary Scattering between Chiral Domains in Chiral Topological Semimetal CoSi
abstract: We evaluate the electron scattering properties in CoSi thin films having either twin (heterochiral) or non-twin (homochiral) grain boundaries using first-principles quantum transport calculations. We find that scattering across a twin grain boundary is more resistive than scattering across a non-twin grain boundary and that non-twin grain boundaries have a greater percentage of surface conduction than twin grain boundaries. This is corroborated by the transmission eigenstate profiles, which show that the surface Fermi-arc electrons can transmit past the non-twin grain boundaries between homochiral domains on the same surface without significant backscattering. In contrast, these surface electrons get scattered along the twin grain boundaries between heterochiral domains to the opposite surface, resulting in partial forward transmission and partial backscattering that yields higher grain-boundary resistivity. This work helps elucidate the complexities of electron transport in chiral topological semimetals for potential application in next-generation nano-interconnects.

title: TexFlow: learning crystallographic texture on SO(3) manifold via normalizing flows
abstract: Crystallographic texture is an important microstructural feature that statistically describes the orientations of grains in polycrystalline materials. Conventional texture analysis relies on the orientation distribution functions and pole figures, which are essential for interpreting the texture of a given material specimen but do not, by themselves, provide a direct framework for predictive modeling of process-structure-property linkages. Data- and machine learning-based approaches offer a means to address this gap; however, a key challenge lies in developing representations and learning frameworks that account for the manifold structure of rotations. In particular, many existing machine learning techniques are designed for Euclidean data and therefore are not readily applicable to rotations in the non-Euclidean group $\text{SO}(3)$. Here we introduce TexFlow, a conditional normalizing flow framework for texture modeling that learns a probability distribution over rotations in $\text{SO}(3)$ by construction. Rotations are encoded in a six-dimensional Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization representation which is then mapped back to valid rotations $\mathbf{R}\in\text{SO}(3)$. The framework supports conditional probabilistic modeling of texture $p(\mathbf{R}|c)$, where $c$ may represent processing parameters like temperature or deformation state. To complement conventional texture-analysis visualizations, such as pole figures and sections of the orientation distribution function, we further introduce Hopf-fibration visualizations as a compact global representation of texture. TexFlow is validated on both unconditional and conditional experimental and simulated texture datasets spanning diverse material systems. We show that TexFlow can accurately capture multimodal textures and their conditional evolution, providing a data-driven framework for establishing process-texture linkages.

title: A terminal-group and fluorination matrix for designing polar nematic liquid crystals
abstract: Lateral fluorination has emerged as a powerful design variable in the design of polar liquid crystals, but its interplay with terminal-group identity remains poorly understood. Here we report a 40-member matrix of biphenyl-ester-phenyl mesogens that independently varies lateral core fluorination and terminal-group identity. Increasing lateral fluorination generally suppresses apolar mesophases and clearing points, however this same change can enable polar nematic phase behaviour in conjunction with suitable terminal units. Graph Fourier analysis of conformer averaged atomic charges shows polar materials occupy a high-frequency region of charge-spectral space, consistent with a bond-scale electrostatic motif. Different terminal units can bias this towards higher or lower frequencies, and in doing so can enable polar order to emerge.

title: Continuously Tunable Mid-Infrared Metalens Integrating Moiré and Pancharatnam-Berry Phases
abstract: A varifocal mid-infrared metalens designed for focusing applications is proposed to integrate both Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) and Moiré pattern-based mechanisms for rotational wavefront control. The metalens employs two identical nanostructured discs featuring germanium (Ge) meta-atoms on calcium fluoride (CaF2) substrates, operating as birefringent half-wave retarders with 99.95% Polarization Conversion Ratio (PCR) and 83.65% total transmission power at 2 μm wavelength. Full-wave numerical simulations demonstrate continuous focal length tunability from 45 μm to 12 μm by rotating the second disk from 30 deg. to 120 deg., corresponding to the numerical aperture values ranging from 22.99% to 68.67%. The proposed metalens maintains reconfigurable focusing regardless of the incident light polarization, while concurrently enabling polarization-controlled operation via a phase-modulation mechanism that yields inverse responses under Right Circular Polarization (RCP) and Left Circular Polarization (LCP) illuminations.

title: Discovering Hidden Predictive States in Kinetic Transport
abstract: How do autonomous macroscopic transport laws emerge from kinetic dynamics, and which hidden degrees of freedom must survive coarse-graining? We address these questions by formulating kinetic state reduction as a problem of predictive sufficiency rather than conventional moment truncation. Starting from Boltzmann transport dynamics, we establish a quantitative connection between unresolved microscopic information, irreducible prediction error, and finite-horizon observability. Microscopic preparations with identical macroscopic observables but distinct subsequent evolution provide direct witnesses of incomplete dynamical closure. We develop an entropy-constrained learned state-reduction framework, demonstrated here through linear projections, that identifies the additional predictive states without prescribing their physical identities and determines their necessity through independent response tests, state deletion, and dynamical consistency. An exactly solvable three-velocity model demonstrates that a hidden higher-order moment can influence future energy transport despite identical initial energy and heat flux. Numerical experiments recover this missing direction and reveal how the required state dimension depends on observation scale, prediction horizon, preparation ensemble, and accuracy. In a synthetic 32-channel Boltzmann system, the learned representation identifies predictive combinations spanning multiple kinetic branches and relaxation groups that are not captured by low-order global moments. We further distinguish observable prediction accuracy from autonomous state closure and quantify the information retained through unresolved memory. These results establish an operational framework for testing the emergence of effective transport laws and identifying the microscopic information required for their predictive validity.

title: Spin-wave circulation in unbounded ferromagnetic film
abstract: A key challenge in spin-wave computing is steering spin waves through circuits without wave distortion or reflections. This often results in 1D propagation scenarios, which hinder applicability in 2D magnonic circuits. We demonstrate experimentally a novel approach using a hard magnetic spherical microparticle to guide spin-waves onto a closed path in a plain thin YIG film. The particle stray field induces a radially symmetrical magnetization landscape, which allows spin-waves to loop around. In parallel, we conducted micromagnetic simulations reproducing the experimental conditions, which confirm the circulation of spin-waves over several loops around the particle. This work demonstrates the possibility to steer spin-waves onto a circular path using inhomogeneous magnetic landscape, as well as advancing scalable spin-wave-based information processing technologies.

title: Variable-Resolution Scattering Reveals Ensemble Properties
abstract: SAXS/SANS determine the size and structure of particles and macromolecules in solution. However, the conventional low-angle determination of the radius of gyration, Rg, cannot separately resolve its scattering-weighted mean and the width of its distribution. Because the apparent Rg includes a contribution from ensemble variance, the distribution width is required even to recover the mean Rg. Here, we introduce TENOR-SAXS, a method for estimating the scattering-weighted width of an Rg distribution by applying two anisotropic digital smearings to a single 2D scattering image. Comparing the smeared images provides curvature information unavailable from the conventional radial profile. The resulting observables require no explicit model of the native instrumental point-spread function and show only weak sensitivity over the range of native resolutions typical of SAXS measurements examined here. Analytical expressions are derived in the low-angle and narrow-distribution limits for ensembles described by a known or independently constrained single-particle form factor. For verification, we simulated scattering by particles with several form factors and ensembles with different size distributions, all agree well with the analytical theory. To leading order, the principal observable depends on the scattering-weighted mean and variance rather than on the distribution's functional form or higher moments. For simulated data corresponding to feasible synchrotron exposure times for biological samples, the distribution width and, expressed as a fraction of its mean, was recovered with a typical discrepancy of ~0.1, while the scattering-weighted mean Rg was recovered with ~2% relative discrepancy. TENOR-SAXS thus provides a framework for estimating ensemble width from existing 2D scattering data without explicit instrumental desmearing and for correcting the variance contribution to the apparent radius

title: Enhancement of Li and Na Storage in Janus HfSSe Monolayers by Co-Induced Electron-Deficient Chalcogen Sites: A First-Principles Study
abstract: The growing demand for high-capacity, fast-charging, and durable rechargeable batteries has intensified the search for advanced electrode materials, with two-dimensional materials offering large surface-to-mass ratios and short ion-diffusion pathways. Here, pristine and Co-doped Janus HfSSe monolayers were investigated as anode materials for Li-ion and Na-ion batteries using first-principles density functional theory. Pristine HfSSe was found to be dynamically stable and exhibited a 0.85 eV band gap, while Co substitution shifted the Fermi level toward the valence-band region. Adsorption of the first Li or Na layer induced metallic behavior, thereby improving charge transport. Co doping strengthened alkali-metal binding, with the most favorable Li and Na adsorption energies changing from -2.6125 and -1.9800 eV to -3.7405 and -3.0529 eV, respectively. Co doping created electron-deficient sites that enhanced Li/Na binding. Co-doped HfSSe accommodated up to four Li layers and three Na layers, increasing the theoretical capacities from 555.43 to 776.19 mAh/g for Li and from 370.29 to 582.14 mAh/g for Na. The average open-circuit voltages were 0.62 V for Li and 0.29-0.30 V for Na, with minimum migration barriers of 0.2153 and 0.1044 eV, respectively. These results identified Co-doped Janus HfSSe as a promising anode material for Li-ion and Na-ion batteries.

title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report
abstract: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.

title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery
abstract: On-chip thermal processing is a key technology for materials discovery across all disciplines of the natural sciences. Here, we present a microfabricated heat-delivery platform that enables reaction-induced localized on-chip annealing up to 1400°C. A buried reactive multilayer combined with a nanometric diffusion barrier provide ultra-fast heating and quenching rates on the order of 10$^6$°C s$^{-1}$ as illustrated by the generation of ultra-high aspect ratio microstructures during rapid-solidification and the stabilization of dopant-free tetragonal zirconia at room temperature. Rapid kinetics also enable the observation of transient states of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts. Our work expands localized high-temperature processing routes and offers a material-independent approach for rapid screening of multidimensional nanomaterials on and off-equilibrium.

title: Ubiquitous Flat Bands in Edge-Inflated Random Graphs
abstract: Flat bands are usually associated with periodic lattice geometries, where destructive interference or chiral-symmetry constraints produce macroscopically degenerate eigenstates. Here we show that flat bands arise generically in a broad class of nonperiodic random networks through a simple edge-inflation procedure. Starting from random regular, Voronoi tessellation, Delaunay triangulation, scale-free, small-world, and Erdös-Rényi seed graphs, each edge is replaced by a finite one-dimensional tight-binding chain, either with fixed length $L$ or with random lengths of mean $\bar L$. Although the original random graphs typically have adjacency matrices of full rank and therefore few or no zero eigenstates, their inflated counterparts exhibit extensive flat bands. The flat-band energies are determined by the eigenstates residing on the chains or, more generally, by the eigenvalues of identical loopless motifs replacing the seed bonds. The corresponding eigenstates are states supported on subsets of the inflated chains formed by destructive interference at the original seed vertices. For zero-energy flat bands, we relate the degeneracy to the graph nullity $η(G)$ and the maximum matching number $ν(G)$. The numerical results support the correspondence $η(G)=N-2ν(G)$, up to small deviations, across the random graph ensembles studied. The fraction of degenerate zero-energy states in inflated random graphs is controlled primarily by the average degree of the seed graph. We further show that the flat bands exhibit characteristic robustness to disorder: disorder on the seed sites and random magnetic flux leave the flat bands essentially unchanged, while bond disorder and disorder on the chain or motif sites broaden them. These results show that flat bands do not require crystalline order, but can emerge as robust consequences of local graph inflation and motif substitution.

title: Quantum Formulation of the Spinterface Model
abstract: We present a fully quantum formulation of the spinterface model for the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect, implemented within the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. The model consists of a gold atom hosting a localised magnetic moment, coupled to a chiral molecular chain with Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and contacted by two non-magnetic leads. The magnetic moment is determined self-consistently from the non-equilibrium electronic distribution, and the spin-resolved transmission is computed from the mean-field Hamiltonian. We show that the interfacial magnetic moment and the chiral Rashba term cooperate to produce large current polarisations that reproduce the key experimental signatures of CISS: high polarisation, a threshold emergence at four total sites followed by interference-modulated growth with chain length, thermal suppression, and sign reversal upon chirality inversion. The central new result of this work is a clean separation of the CISS effect into an even (achiral) and an odd (chiral) contribution to the spin current, $I_{S_z}(φ) = I_{S_z}^{\rm even}(φ) + I_{S_z}^{\rm odd}(φ)$. We demonstrate that $I_{S_z}^{\rm odd}$ vanishes exactly at fixed $m_z$ for chains of fewer than four sites and becomes non-zero for chains of four or more sites, with the smallest junction exhibiting a non-zero odd part being the four-site geometry (one gold atom plus three molecular sites). The odd part arises from reciprocity breaking in a device that is simultaneously chiral, magnetically asymmetric (moment on the gold end only), and long enough to support two or more Rashba-active bonds. This provides a direct, parameter-free test of whether an observed spin signal is genuinely chiral or arises from an achiral spin-valve mechanism.

title: Orbital-angular-momentum control of localized Floquet states and photocurrents in Weyl semimetals
abstract: Structured light provides a route to controlling quantum materials not only through its polarization, but also through its spatial profile and orbital angular momentum (OAM). We develop real space theories of a Weyl semimetal driven by a vortex beam and show that optical OAM generates highly localized Floquet vortex states with pronounced circulating photocurrents. Exploiting cylindrical symmetry, we derive a Bogoliubov-de Gennes-like radial equation that resolves the states by angular momentum and reveals their evolution between the light-dressed Weyl cones. For Laguerre-Gaussian beams, the spatially varying drive produces strong hybridization between localized vortex states and bulk states. We complement this continuum description with a Wilson-lattice formulation that retains the full two-dimensional spatial structure and enables direct calculation of local photocurrents. Both approaches consistently identify OAM-induced vortex states localized around the beam axis. The lattice calculation further shows that these states support substantially stronger circulating current densities than the more extended surface states, with the largest current densities associated with the most strongly localized, low-angular-momentum vortex modes. Our results establish optical OAM as a tunable control parameter for creating and manipulating localized current-carrying states in Weyl systems and provide a real-space framework for studying photocurrents generated by spatially structured light.

title: Capturing Open Quantum System Dynamics with Compact Dressed Hamiltonians
abstract: We advance the compact dressed Hamiltonian (CDH) framework to simulate the dynamics of open quantum systems strongly coupled to structured bosonic environments. The CDH approach combines reaction-coordinate mapping with a polaron transformation, incorporating strong system-environment hybridization into a dressed representation before truncating the collective bosonic mode. As a result of this truncation, dynamical features are captured with substantially fewer states than in the original representation. The residual environment is treated using a weak-coupling Markovian quantum master equation. We benchmark the method for spin-boson-type models including a single spin, coupled spins, and spin ensembles, considering both resonant and off-resonant regimes and weak to strong system-bath coupling. Comparisons with hierarchical equations of motion and converged reaction-coordinate calculations demonstrate that the CDH representation systematically approaches the reference dynamics with a compact Hilbert space, accurately reproducing oscillation frequencies, relaxation behavior, and long-time populations over a broad parameter regime. The method further captures cooperative phenomena, including bath-mediated interactions, synchronization between spins, and signatures for collective emission. Beyond efficient time propagation, the CDH framework provides direct access to the spectrum and eigenmodes of the Liouvillian. We demonstrate that slow dynamical modes converge rapidly in the CDH representation, enabling identification of relaxation timescales without fitting time-dependent observables. As a whole, the CDH framework provides an efficient and physical description of strongly coupled open quantum-system dynamics.

title: Electronic driving of torsional modes in carbon nanotubes via orbital-phonon coupling
abstract: We theoretically investigate electronic driving of a torsional mode in a suspended carbon nanotube quantum dot. The valley states in a nanotube carry opposite orbital magnetic moments along the tube axis, and intervalley mixing forms valley-mixed eigenstates whose splitting can be controlled by an axial magnetic field. We formulate an orbital-rotation coupling between the torsional angular velocity and the valley orbital angular momentum. Using a master equation for sequential tunneling through normal-metal electrodes, we calculate the steady-state current and the phonon distribution of the torsional mode. When the valley-state splitting matches the torsional phonon energy, orbital transitions can drive the mode out of equilibrium. The contacts control both phonon pumping and its electrical readout, allowing substantial excitation with a positive, vanishing, or negative current response. The mechanism requires no intrinsic spin or valley polarization of the electrodes, but uses state-dependent tunneling at the contacts.

title: A Comparative Study of LED Lighting Control Strategies for Energy-Efficient Greenhouse Operations
abstract: Greenhouse supplemental lighting is essential for meeting crop Daily Light Integral (DLI) requirement. However, conventional always-on and rule-based strategies are inherently energy-inefficient since they ignore future sunlight availability. This paper reports the results of deploying various supplemental lighting control strategies, namely, always-on, always-off, heuristic, optimal prediction-based, and two peak-shift variants, simultaneously in a single greenhouse at the Hampton Roads AREC of Virginia Tech, to ensure that every treatment experiences identical conditions. %The shared infrastructure is built on an MQTT-based IoT platform with Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density (PPFD) sensing and PWM-driven LED control; The prediction-based and peak-shift strategies optimize LED schedules using a Markov chain-based solar forecast. Experimental results over two replicates %(20~February--15~April~2026, 72~plants per treatment) show that the prediction-based strategy meets the desired DLI target at 65\% cost reduction relative to the always-on baseline while achieving the highest dry-mass yield among the proposed adaptive strategies. The heuristic strategy incurs only a 6\% cost premium over prediction-based control, offering a competitive forecast-free alternative. The peak-shift variants achieve the lowest active-strategy costs by shifting LED demand into off-peak tariff windows. A yield-per-dollar efficiency metric is finally introduced to jointly capture energy cost and crop output showing that the prediction-based strategy ranks highest at 18.976~g/\$, more than double the always-on value of 9.391~g/\$. These findings can provide greenhouse operators with an evidence-based framework for selecting a lighting control approach that balances energy cost, crop quality, and system complexity.

title: Attracting Rotations Obstruct Almost-Global Consensus on Spheres over Strongly Connected Graphs
abstract: We study discrete-time consensus on the Euclidean unit sphere, where weighted combinations of neighboring states are normalized to unit length. For symmetric weights on connected undirected graphs and ambient dimension $d\ge3$, earlier results establish instability of non-consensus fixed points under suitable weight conditions. For directed graphs on the unit circle, earlier results show that fixed points other than consensus and antipodal configurations occur only for a measure-zero set of weights. We show that these conclusions do not extend directly to general strongly connected directed graphs in higher dimensions. First, we construct full-rank non-consensus fixed points whose tangent eigenvalues all equal one, showing that strict linear instability need not hold. In a separate construction, for every $d\ge3$, we present a sparse strongly connected graph admitting full-rank fixed points on an open set of its permitted weights. Our main result establishes robust counterexamples to almost-global consensus: attracting rotating motions exist for $d=2$ with every $n\ge3$ and for $d=3$ with every $n\ge6$. These motions are locally asymptotically stable modulo common rotations and have asymptotic phase. They persist on open sets of strictly positive weight matrices. For each such matrix, an open set of initial configurations approaches neither consensus nor any fixed configuration. Thus the absence of full-rank non-consensus fixed points does not ensure almost-global convergence to consensus.

title: Continuous-Time Policy Gradient from Discrete Data: Convergence Analysis and Model-Free Algorithms
abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning seeks an optimal policy under unknown dynamics driven by stochastic differential equations using observations collected at discrete times. We develop a policy gradient framework that combines rigorous convergence analysis with learning from discrete data. We first establish a performance difference lemma and derive policy gradient formulas for randomized and parametrized policies. We then prove exponential convergence of an entropy-regularized policy flow to the regularized optimum. For discrete parametrized updates, we derive a convergence bound that explicitly separates the contributions of critic error, policy-regression error, and the learning step size. To enable learning under unknown dynamics, we integrate this framework with PhiBE, which constructs a continuous-time surrogate generator from discrete transition data. The resulting on-policy and off-policy model-free actor-critic algorithms preserve the continuous-time structure of the control problem. Numerical experiments on an entropy-regularized linear-quadratic regulator and a nonlinear wheeled robot demonstrate the performance and stability of the proposed methods with both known and data-driven dynamics.

title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings. To address this gap, we study SGD dynamics in deep linear neural networks - simplified models that retain key non-convex characteristics while remaining analytically tractable. Building on recent results for gradient descent, we extend convergence guarantees to SGD under regularized squared loss. We establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates. Using the framework of asymptotic pseudotrajectories from stochastic approximation theory, our analysis establishes then, for both deterministic and adaptive step-size choices, convergence of SGD to the set of critical points under mild conditions (without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data). To our knowledge, this is the first work providing almost sure convergence guarantees for SGD in deep linear networks, bridging the gap between theoretical optimization and practical stochastic training.

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
abstract: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface
abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.

title: Wavepackets in subsonic elliptical jets: coherent-structure eduction and linear modelling
abstract: We study coherent structures extracted from time-resolved particle image velocimetry (TR-PIV) measurements of isothermal elliptical jets with aspect ratio of 1:2, at Mach numbers 0.4 and 0.7. The velocity snapshots are decomposed according to the D$_2$ symmetry. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) is then used to identify coherent structures. Modelling is performed using three-dimensional parabolised stability equations (3D-PSE) based on linearisation about the time-averaged mean flows. A comparison between SPOD and 3D-PSE results shows alignment of SPOD and single-mode PSE structures of up to 70\%. A linear combination of PSE solutions, obtained from the family of initially unstable local modes, leads to SPOD-PSE alignment of up to 90\%. Limitations are observed at low frequencies and near the nozzle and are attributed to the existence of non-modal amplification mechanisms. The study shows that coherent structures in turbulent elliptical jets can be educed using the D$_2$-SPOD approach, and modelled using 3D PSE.

title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

title: Restraint-Induced Loss in Software-Intensive Enterprises: Large A Verified Technical Economic Impact Model of Operational Downtime and Delayed Commercialization, with Tail-Risk Security Sizing and Three Enterprise Case Studies
abstract: When an enterprise must stop using a software component (for example, because of an interim court restraint in a technology patent dispute), the economic loss passes through a chain of technical mechanisms. Withdrawing the component exposes dependent capabilities. Fallback paths degrade throughput, correctness or feature coverage. Incident rates and recovery backlogs rise. Customers respond. Remediation programmes compete against the restraint clock, and planned launches are pushed back. This paper develops and verifies a \emph{technical--economic impact model} (TEIM) that quantifies this chain end to end as a probability distribution of present-value loss rather than as a point estimate. The technical layer combines (i)~a lattice-valued, fixed-point semantics of service dependencies with degraded fallbacks, (ii)~continuous-time Markov reliability models evaluated by uniformization and specified in continuous stochastic logic, and (iii)~a fluid queueing model of post-outage backlog. These feed (iv)~convex acute-outage loss functions with regulatory and contractual thresholds, (v)~compound-Poisson excess-incident processes, (vi)~survival-weighted functional, attrition and funding channels that provably avoid double counting, (vii)~a real-options valuation of forcibly delayed launches with an explicit closed form, and (viii)~a COCOMO~II--driven stochastic activity network for design-around and substitution strategies. We prove seven theorems and eight propositions.

title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.

title: Observability-Aligned Diffusion and Null-Space Completion for EEG Source Localization
abstract: Electrophysiological source imaging is severely underdetermined because the lead-field matrix has limited rank relative to the source dimension and strongly correlated columns. Scalp EEG measurements constrain only the observable row-space component, leaving a high-dimensional null space unobservable. We propose a two-stage framework coupling posterior diffusion refinement with deterministic null-space completion. A minimum-norm-initialized, singular-coordinate Posterior-DDIM sampler combines a spatiotemporal diffusion prior with direction-dependent measurement reliability to refine the observable component. A frozen ridge predictor and nonlinear temporal residual network then estimate the null component under explicit projection constraints, preserving the refined row estimate and its predicted EEG exactly. All learned components are trained exclusively on simulated cortical activity and its row-null decomposition, without paired EEG-source training data. Across simulations with varying noise levels, the method achieved higher frame-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision, together with lower localization error, than conventional and learning-based baselines. Exploratory evaluations on evoked EEG and simultaneous scalp EEG-stereo-EEG recordings showed condition- and event-dependent concordance with cross-modal and intracranial references.

title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method
abstract: Shipboard equipment must survive the transient loads of underwater explosions. The U.S. Navy certifies such equipment with the Dynamic Design Analysis Method (DDAM), a modal response analysis driven by Navy shock design spectra. DDAM is well established as a verification tool, yet it is rarely used as a design driver in topology optimization. The design spectrum depends on the modal mass, a non-smooth coupling that classical sensitivity formulations do not address. This paper presents a complete differentiable formulation of the DDAM criterion for gradient-based topology optimization. Eigenvalue sensitivities follow the Fox-Kapoor method, and eigenvector sensitivities follow Nelson's method. The chain rule covers a spectral displacement that depends on both the natural frequency and the modal participation factor. Automatic differentiation assembles the sensitivity, and the engineer can certify components inside the optimization loop rather than after design. Three certification problems on a representative shipboard equipment frame demonstrate the workflow. In each, the optimizer removes 43.2% to 46.1% of the design-domain material and holds the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable. Two companion studies follow. A compliance-optimized frame of nearly the same mass has a 5.2 Hz fundamental, outside the range the certification can qualify. Its nominal response also exceeds the allowable by a factor of 2.75. A lower bound on the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues separates the repeated pair that the demonstrations drive onto the frequency floor. The response then stops oscillating across the acceptance boundary. It ends at most 0.5% above the allowable, at a cost of under two percentage points of volume fraction.
